utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could remind you, Mr. Krasniqi, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. I think Mr. Topolski has a few more questions. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yesterday at the end of the session you gave us a detailed comment from a paragraph I read to you of a witness, Susan Pedersen. To lead on to the next topic, which is detention and arrests, I wonder if I could just visit again that paragraph or part of it. What she says, Mr. Krasniqi, is that she and the organisation of which she was a part got the impression that abductions or arrests committed by the KLA were - and these are the words I want to focus on if I may - "systematic, preplanned, and organised." Now, Mr. Krasniqi, you've given us a detailed response to this, but I just want to ask you this question: Were you ever a part of or a party to any conversation or meeting with any KLA colleague in which a system, a plan, or the organisation of detentions or arrests of innocent civilians was discussed?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There has been no meeting of such a nature and we never dealt with such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And in an attempt, Mr. Krasniqi, to lay a ghost for the future so is there will be no misunderstanding about it, when you say "there has been no meeting of such a nature," may I broaden it, please, to ask you to be clear whether there was ever any discussion or conversation as between you and colleagues regarding a system, a plan, an organisation?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no and I don't have anything to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That leads us on to the third of the topics I want to talk to you about, and it's a very brief topic, Mr. Krasniqi, and it's detention and arrests. And here one is talking about civilians, non-combatants. You'll recollect the distinction that you agreed with yesterday. Was it regarded amongst the KLA as being legitimate to stop, detain, and question people during the war?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. During the war, people have been stopped. For example, journalists who came to the areas where the KLA was there and they have been stopped. It was necessary to stop them and ask them why they came there. There might have been a case or two when a Serb citizen might have entered our areas. And after they have been asked questions they were released. And this happened only in our areas, but they were released. But still, I would like to say that the main roads were still under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to that under the fifth of the topics, which is territorial control. But can I move on, then, to the next topic, which is structure. And, Mr. Krasniqi, what I have in mind to ask you is one or two questions regarding structure and organisation of the KLA up to the end of August 1998. The reason I have chosen that date or month is because I suggest, and we have had other evidence to this effect, that brigades and battalions were formed or began to be formed at the end of the August of 1998. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, then let's please look together, can we, at elements of structure and organisation up to, but not including, that re-organisation. First of all, I imagine you would agree with the proposition that what the KLA was certainly up until then could properly be described as a guerrilla army. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that until March and April of 1998, the KLA was a guerrilla army and then it expanded. There was mobilisation of people, recruitment, and for some time we had a voluntary army. And the General Staff had the responsibility to organise this voluntary army. From April it was a voluntary army, from April till the end of August or the beginning of September. So it was mainly a voluntary army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I take issue with that last answer or parts of it. I suggest that the KLA was never anything other than a voluntary army. There was never conscription into the KLA at any stage, was there?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "mobilisation" I don't mean it in the sense of conscription. I explained in the previous sessions, it was -- by "mobilisation" I mean voluntary mobilisation, solidarity with the fight that was being waged by the soldiers of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I follow that. But at the beginning of that last answer you said "I had already said until March and April of 1998 the KLA was a guerrilla army and then it expanded," and then you went on to deal with mobilisation. In terms of the tactics of the KLA up to, including, and, I suggest, beyond the battle at Rahovec we were talking about yesterday, it was employing very much, was it not, guerrilla-type military tactics, hit-and-run, that sort of thing. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It had, did it not - and again we are still in this period, please, up to the end of August 1998 - it had what I've described and I think you have elsewhere as a horizontal command structure. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It had no rigid hierarchical structure, did it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it didn't. It was not possible to have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Indeed it suffered, if that's the right word, certainly in this period if not beyond it with perhaps one if not more than one separate internal faction, did it not? And I have in mind FARK, F-A-R-K. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you've stressed to us more than once that your role and function was political and not military. I don't want to waste yours or anyone else's time. Are you able to assist us if I was to ask you questions about the early creation of firing positions, units, points, and so on and so forth? Can you assist the Tribunal on those matters or are you not able to do so, given your experience?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the question must be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I was just trying to see if we could deal with the topic together. Let me ask you the question and see if you can help us. In this period we are talking about, members of the KLA would gather together, wouldn't they, in villages predominantly, in order to protect them from Serb assault. That would be the position in the early days, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the early days after March?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That period, March, April, May, June.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was mainly a voluntary organisation of people, or people who wanted to fight for the freedom of the country and the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this willingness to fight grew and at that time some kind of organisation began and the village's guards were established and some of them were also armed with hunting rifles, as I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And we've heard other evidence about that. Of course one of the situations that was being confronted then, was it not, was that some of the people who came to volunteer had some military experience, but many did not. That was the situation in those early days, was it not, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was. In the first days, the early days, and the last days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. So a group of men gathering together to, in my example, say protect a village would make their own decisions on the ground, would they not, as to the taking up of defensive positions and so on in a very informal, very fluid way, I suggest, Mr. Krasniqi. Is that the position as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was, and that's why the General Staff had to commit itself to organise these people in a better form of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Communication within a group of KLA men even within a village and certainly communication with KLA operators in other villages was primitive to say the least of it, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether primitive is the right word to use, but the communication was based on the willingness of people to fight against the occupiers and their police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Leaders of these groups emerged; they were not appointed from on high. That is right, isn't it? They emerged usually from the groups themselves, the men who ended up leading those groups I mean. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was. In the majority of the cases, we have followed how people were chosen in those positions, but it was on the basis of the contribution they had given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I move on then to the next topic, please, from structure, and it's territorial control of the KLA or lack of it. Again, I'm dealing with the same period, to the end of August 1998, Mr. Krasniqi. Yesterday you were good enough to concede that your claim in the Der Speigel interview that the KLA controlled 40 per cent of the country was not accurate. You remember telling us that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Dealing with the ability of the KLA in this period to communicate one unit to another, one of the problems, was it not, was that units of the KLA - before the formation of the brigades and battalions and so on, so before the end of August 1998 - one of the major problems was many of these units were very far apart geographically. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Indeed, yesterday -- you may remember answering Mr. Whiting's questions about International Red Cross documents and you may recall telling us that you had to send these documents where you could via couriers, your word, or use the communique as a method of attempting to communicate the contents of these documents to KLA fighters. Have I accurately summarised the position, Mr. Krasniqi, as you indicated it to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I use the word, and I took me up on it a few moments ago, primitive communication systems. Again, this goes under the heading of territorial control. Radio communication. Again focusing on this period, that was, was it not, limited as between units or groups of the KLA at this stage. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did there become in due course places that were regarded as centres for radio communication of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was such a centre, yes, placed in Kosmac mountain in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And in the Kosmac mountain in Drenica, were there broadcasts, as it were, by a radio station? Is that what it was in effect?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a radio walkie-talkie system, but the mountain was very high. They -- the signal went to other peaks of mountains and that's how the communication was established in all the cases when the Serbian army and police attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And, for example, the call to arms, the call for assistance to Rahovec came from that radio transmitter, did it, in mid-July 1998? I take but one example.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- as I said before, we did not have a radio. We used the system that the police army -- that the police and the army -- Serb police and army used. And sometimes they also intercepted and blocked this form of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I follow. But would it have been from that radio base in Kosmac that you've described that the call for assistance to Rahovec would have come, Mr. Krasniqi, or cannot you say?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rahovec is situated in the Bjeshket e Zatriqit. There were people there who had walkie-talkies and they could have a connection to Kosmac and they were aware of what was going on in -- within KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: While we're on Rahovec, I wonder if I could go back to something you were talking about yesterday, again when Mr. Whiting was asking you questions. And I'm looking, if anyone wants to go back, to page 47 and 48 of the transcript yesterday. You told us about the fighting at Rahovec and you linked it to fighting elsewhere. What you were telling us yesterday, Mr. Krasniqi, was that we, that is to say the General Staff of the KLA, did not authorise the attack because you lacked weapons necessary to the liberation of these towns. I want to see if I have understood it correctly. Are you saying that the beginning of the fighting in Rahovec was spontaneous and unauthorised as far as the General Staff was concerned? Is that what you're saying about it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If I were to add the adjective to that list of spontaneous and unauthorised as also reckless on the part of the KLA at that stage, Mr. Krasniqi, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And remind us, please: What was the date of the beginning of this battle that we are about at Rahovec, as best as you can recollect it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Will I be right in suggesting to you that it was sometime in the middle of July, 16th, 17th, or 18th, thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been the middle of July, but I can't remember the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. We can move on to the last of the topics I want to deal with, Mr. Krasniqi, and I'm sure you don't remember what it is, so I will remind you. It is Serbian state security. Now, I want to put three propositions to you regarding Serbian state security. And I ask you these questions both as -- in your capacity as you became a spokesman of the KLA but also, of course, as a citizen of Kosova and as a internee, as it were, for a long period of time at one stage of your life. The first proposition is this, Mr. Krasniqi: Do you agree that Serbian state security apparatus was a sophisticated machine?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was very well-equipped and very well supported financially by Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, both the army, the police, and the secret service. Belgrade was a kind of superpower in all those respects in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It was - and of course I focus as it were on its secret service wing - it was, my third proposition, very experienced in dealing with its own population, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had long experience of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I wonder if we can attempt to compare it with another well-known organisation that operated until 1989 in Eastern Germany, the Stasi, I have in mind. The Stasi, I suggest, was an organisation that used as one of its tools the idea that citizens would spy and inform on other citizens to a very significant degree. In terms of your experience and knowledge of life in Kosovo up to and including the time we are dealing with in this court, would that compare with the way in which Serbian state security operated or would you in any way distinguish it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say and I believe that it was similar. The Serbian secret service was even more sophisticated of that of Eastern Germany. I will give one figure here: From 1981 to 1991, in ten years the secret service have dealt with 7.000 Albanians who have given various information. After 1991, many Albanians left Kosovo because of this activity of the Serbian secret service. It is precisely the secret service information that I'm giving you now that after 1991 we dealt with more Albanians than we dealt before 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I follow. Is it within your experience - and I'm now dealing with the period up to and including the war - is it within your experience and knowledge, Mr. Krasniqi, that some state security operations were conducted where people were killed and blame was attributed to the KLA? Did that --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been attempts of this nature. For example, by the end of the war in Kosovo there was a killing -- a professor of the university was killed. He was a high politician of the Democratic League. He was a Serb and he was a member of the Rambouillet delegation. And the state security service tried to blame this killing on the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. I want to look at another topic under this same heading, if I may, and I am picking up something you said to us yesterday at page 24 of the transcript. You were talking about people being held and detained and so on. "I'm convinced," you said to us yesterday, "that the Belgrade regime had infiltrated within its ranks unarmed people." I want to be clear what you're saying or attempting to say to us there, Mr. Krasniqi. Are you suggesting that the Belgrade regime infiltrated into the ranks of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we keep in mind the very professional organisation of that service, they had ample opportunity to infiltrate their people in the ranks of the KLA and I gave here examples of people who have left the war zones and they were captured by the Serbian police. And we don't know anything about their fate, even today. These people had been spied upon by the secret service people who were operating, maybe even in the ranks, inside the ranks of the KLA. However, I would like to say that even in the areas where the KLA was in control, they still had people operating there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Again, on your first day of evidence on the same topic at page 43 of the transcript you said this: "Many people at that time, even today, are in connection with Serb secret service." Mr. Krasniqi, I want to look at that with you just for a moment as my last questions for you. Do you literally mean that to be true, that today there are people working for the Serb secret service within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although this is not inside my area of responsibility, I am convinced that the secret service -- the Serbian secret service in Kosovo is still very powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You come to us, sir, from a position of importance and responsibility within your own country as a leading politician, if I may say so, a member of your parliament, the leader of the opposition. I want to be clear what you're saying. What do you say would be the current aims of the Serb secret service working within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aim of that service in Kosovo -- first of all, you have to keep in mind that they have operated in Kosovo for 90 years, more or less. They want to keep alive their ancient policies over Kosovo to destabilise the situation, the political situation and the security situation. And for that reason during these five or six years they have exploited Kosovo citizens, manipulating them, not allowing them to integrate into the positive changes that have occurred in the country. So the operations of this service aim at destabilising the country politically to show to the world that Kosovo is not a safe country for its own citizens and neither Albanians nor the international community are not [as interpreted] able to keep the country safe, to have free movement of the citizens. So these are the aims of this service, multiple aims. They want to destabilise Kosovo, to make Kosovo an unsafe place for all its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, finally, from the general to the specific, Mr. Krasniqi. And when I mean specific, what I mean is the possible connection with what you've just been saying between that and this very trial conducted by this Tribunal. And I do so because it's something you said very early on in your evidence and I want to read it back to you from the transcript. "I believe," you said, "that the indictment," page 7 of the transcript. "I believe that the indictment against the accused has been built on politically motivated evidence given by people who have been in the service of the violent occupiers in Kosovo." Mr. Krasniqi, I sought to promise you at the outset of my questions yesterday precise questions and invited precise answers. May I put this to you in light of what you said to us within minutes of taking the witness stand and your answers now: Is this the position, as far as you are concerned, that it would not be safe for this Tribunal to rule out the possibility that evidence given here by some citizens of Kosovo has been or may have been influenced by Serbian secret service?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I see Mr. Whiting is on his feet so you better not answer for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this question. When Mr. Topolski started this line of questioning, the witness clearly stated this is outside his area of responsibility. And so what is being asked here, I would submit, is just rank speculation on the part of the witness without any basis in -- without any foundation about other witnesses who have come here and other evidence that has been presented here to the Court. If there's a foundation for it, perhaps; but I don't think the witness should be permitted to engage in just pure speculation about other witnesses who have come here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: First of all, although the objection is not taken on this ground, the relevance of it as far as this defendant and I suggest other defendants concerned is that which I opened all those weeks and months ago, that one of the areas this Court should and no doubt will examine is the possibility of collusion as between witnesses or the influence of this organisation on the testimony the witnesses come to this Tribunal to give. What this witness said in-chief was after the line I've just quoted: "I am a witness that they have been processed in advance before they were given to the Prosecutors of the Tribunal. They have been processed by the Serb intelligence service." It's upon that answer that he gave, this witness coming from where he comes from, with his background and present position would not, I respectfully submit, have said such a thing lightly nor flippantly. And if it be that the Court would wish me to seek to establish whether he has, as it were, the wherewithal to answer my question, then of course I shall not hesitate to do so. But it was upon the basis of what he said that I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please proceed on the basis you've indicated, Mr. Topolski, that is to see what might be the factual foundation for that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krasniqi, you've heard that exchange and what I want to do is ask you this: You said to us when you came to that change about politically motivated evidence of people who have been in the service of the violent occupiers, these words, and I quote you: "I am a witness that they have been processed in advance before given -- before they were given to the Prosecutors of the Tribunal. They have been processed by the Serb intelligence service." Now, sir, was that an answer honestly given on the first day of your evidence from that chair?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my evidence, I think I have given it honestly. I was very concrete in my answers and I tried to back everything that I said with facts. If I'm asking to argue this again, I can provide you with new facts that will prove that my believe is based on facts and only facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good, because we are interested only in facts and not upon speculation, gossip, or rumour, Mr. Krasniqi. Tell this Tribunal, please, if you are able to do so. Upon what facts do you base the assertion that people have been processed before giving evidence to the Prosecutors of this Tribunal by Serb intelligence services? What are the facts?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base this on many witnesses that have come here to give evidence, on many witnesses that have been part of trial proceedings in Kosova, and on the fact that there were attempts even here to give the war of the Albanian people of Kosova a direction that was not in reality. I base this also on the fact that for all the crimes committed in Kosova before the war and during the war by the Serbian police and military forces, there hasn't been any legal proceedings about these crimes, there hasn't been even prosecution of these crimes. Nobody from the ranks of the Serbian soldiers, from the Serbian leaders, has been held responsible for the crimes that have been committed. And I say that all this is based on the evidence of the Serbian servants and those who serve this secret service. There has been attempt during these years by the political forces in Kosovo to engage in the political developments and to favour those prosecutors and legal workers who worked before in the -- during the Serbian regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be one element of that that might have potential, otherwise not. That is the first line or so of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "Witnesses that have come here to give evidence." I'm not sure what may lie --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No. And out of an abundance of caution it may be appropriate to go to private session to examine that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, the meaning of private session is that no one outside this room can nor will hear of what is taking place.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of that answer that you just gave us that "witnesses have come here to give evidence." Mr. Krasniqi, I repeat, we are only interested in facts and not speculation. Are you in a position to give this Tribunal any names of any witnesses you suggest have come here to give evidence influenced by the Serb secret service? Just answer that question yes or no, please, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Witnesses that gave evidence not by their real names but with coded names, those who gave evidence before this Trial Chamber, they were in close connection with the Serb secret service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Again, just answer this next question yes or no. Do you know the real identities of any of those people? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their real names, but I know their evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to be clear, please, sir, if I may. Are you saying that the fact that they gave evidence anonymously indicates that they are working or their evidence may in some way be potentially influenced by the Serb secret service? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And that is a genuine position that you hold, is it, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only my opinion, but since I am speaking on my behalf this is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if that would be in the Tribunal's view a sufficient basis to enable me to put the proposition that I was seeking to end my cross-examination with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber takes the view it's not a basis that would be adequate, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have no other questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi, for your patience. That's all I ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not sure where I should now look. To Mr. Mansfield. We should go back in public session I think, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, good afternoon. I represent Fatmir Limaj, who sits behind me to my right. You'll be pleased to know I don't have a great deal to ask you. A lot of ground has been covered and hopefully I'll be able to do it within the hour so you know how much there is. I'm sorry about this. I want to start, if I may, by asking you about Fatmir Limaj as a person. You indicated yesterday that you met him in June and you met him on a few occasions after that and no doubt you've met him after the war was over before he was brought here to this Tribunal. What I want to ask you is this: Could you first of all indicate your overall view of Fatmir Limaj as a person, please.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you expand and just tell us what your view is.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said before in the previous session, in the second I think it was, yesterday, I've known Fatmir Limaj since June 1998. And later on, especially after October and November 1998, I got to know him even better due to the fact we both were members of the General Staff of the Kosova Liberation Army. Throughout this time, he has been a close friend of mine, a good friend, and a great communicator with the citizens. And he has supported a lot the citizens, especially those who during the Serb offensives took shelter in the -- in the valleys of Berisa Mountains, in the valleys above the villages of Kishna Reka, Nekovce, Bajice, Shale, and Kroimire. On these gorges and during the frequent offensives launched by the Serbs, there were around 60.000 to 70.000 civilians seeking shelter, mainly of them -- mainly women, children, and elderly persons. There were persons of other ages as well, due to the lack of weapons and means to arm them. The help and aid that he provided to the civilian population is such that he should be in a different position and compensated for what he did; however, things happen in life. His presence here is unbearable for his family, for himself, and for us as his friends; yet, we think in these moments positive democratic process is taking place in Kosova, his absence in these processes is very evident. I'm telling you sincerely that his absence is very evident also in the process of reconciliation between the Kosova citizens of different nationalities, a reconciliation that has been the aim and the goal of this Tribunal. We believe that the truth and the facts are in Fatmir's favour and that he should come back and return to his life. As Israel [as interpreted] -- Disrael [as interpreted] would put it, life is very short and should be lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think there may be, looking at the transcript -- I think it should be Disraeli rather than Israel. I'm not sure. I think it's Disraeli. I think a number of us would agree that quotation. Could it be changed from Israel to Disraeli, so that the transcript can be accurate. I'll move on. You've indicated that he was not a member of the General Staff until November of 1998. I want to work backwards, if I may, concentrating on Fatmir Limaj. The period between August and November saw the establishment of brigades and in his case the one relevant to him is Brigade 121, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We also know and I'm not going to take up time with you, that the territory occupied, if I can put it this way or at least within the bounds of 121, was not identical to the zones or subzones that have existed before August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to move backwards again to the period up to the end of August about which you were asked a few questions this afternoon and several before that, the period being between roughly April and August. There were in existence theoretically seven subzones which you mentioned on a previous occasion. That is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'll come to the extent to which zones or operational and active in that period in one moment. However, it's right to say that Fatmir Limaj was not a commander in charge of any of the zones, however active or inactive, during that period, was he?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The extent to which any one of the seven zones was operational in that period was to a large extent itself dependent on how organised the subzones had been before April of 1998. So, for example, Drenica had been very organised before or more organised and was in a better position to become active after April. Is that a fair description?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And in fact I don't know whether you can attempt a league table of the seven, but that may be a little unrealistic. The reason I ask you is this: An answer that you gave to the Prosecution was that the Pastrik zone in the period April through to August was lagging behind in terms of attempting any kind of organisation. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said this. And if necessary, I can speak of the organisation of each and every zone when it started to expand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to concentrate, if I may. I think Drenica is at the top. Of the seven zones, is it possible for you to indicate where Pastrik may come in terms of organisation and development? Is it near the bottom of the seven or is it near the middle or where is it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: In the middle. And in the Pastrik zone there were -- were there several units so far as you could tell, again in the April to August period, several units began to spring up and operate there?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, can you indicate the names of any of the units that were operating in that zone during that period? That's April to August, before the brigades were established.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can name some, not all of them. There existed in the Malisheve municipality the Lumi unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Rahovec municipality in the Zatriq mountain there was a unit called 500; it was called after a number. There was another unit in Therande municipality, former Suva Reka; it was called Lisi. And also another unit in Prizren municipality in the village of Vrini, but I don't remember the name of this unit. There were smaller units as well, but I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just on that answer you've given so far, was the Lisi unit otherwise known as tree and Lumi as river? Just asking for clarification. Sorry to ask that. Is that another name for the same units, in other words tree in English for lisi and luma [sic] for river?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You can't remember some of the others. Was -- I just want to ask you about Celiku. Was that a unit you were familiar with or units?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the unit that was led by Fatmir Limaj. It was based in Klecke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if we could just develop that a little. In this period April through to August, you've described this as the second stage in the development of the KLA, in other words the stage between it acting as a guerrilla army which targeted precise actions and precise places and people, into a movement of people towards the KLA which you've described as voluntary and then obviously the later stage it becomes more like a regular army. So it's the middle stage. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And from everything you've said so far, it appears that during this voluntary phase, what -- the major problem for the KLA was a lack of infrastructure, resources, funds, arms, and communication that could cope with the influx of people who wanted to provide resistance. Is that a fair description?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what it meant in practical terms was that first of all the higher commands such as existed, the mobile General Staff that moved around - you've already described it - they wouldn't know necessarily how many people had volunteered, where they were, or who had been elected amongst them to be their leaders always. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Similarly if one moves down a level to the units, I'll call them units, operating as people volunteered, the individual units were groups, they wouldn't know necessarily how many other people were volunteering in other units on the other side of a mountain, would they?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And in these circumstances that we've just gone through, do you agree that the element of control, therefore, was a both confused and difficult exercise?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And -- I'm sorry just to repeat the question; there are two parts to it. It was difficult and also confused during this period?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult, it was confused, and the division made by the Serbian police and army forces made this even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if you could be provided - you may have seen it before - with the maps that we have which are identified as P1. And if there isn't one in front of you, it will come. And in particular, I want to turn to map 6 in P1. If you would kindly turn to map 6, you'll find they're all numbered in slightly different places, but it's map 6 with villages and red dots all over it. It's about the seventh map in, in fact. Now you have the map 6 in front of you. You will see if you -- well, I'll do it this way. Lapusnik's in a square, a red square. And then below that is Berisa with a red triangle. So I'm coming down in a straight line you can see, until we get to Klecka. Can you see Klecka with a red dot?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, this next question you may not be able to help with. I don't know whether you can. The question is this: Do you happen to know during the April to August period the villages which the particular unit under the command of Fatmir Limaj, Celiku unit, where he went to help other groups? For example, if you look to the left as you're looking at the plan, in other words westwards, you'll see Ladrovac and then you'll see Terpeze just beyond that. If I go through the villages, are you able to help with this or not? The villages that his unit assisted or that he assisted?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how he assisted the citizens or when he went as assistance to other groups during attacks by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I mean the former. In other words, when he was going to assist citizens and help with the gradual growth of other units of resistance and so on. During the April to August period the villages he would go to -- I've started with the ones just to the west there. There are ones further to the south, Malisheve, Banje, Bajice. If you can't say, I won't pursue it. But I wanted to ask you if you happened to know during Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this period if those were the villages which he was concentrating on, firstly for helping citizens, and secondly citizens to protect themselves against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my recollection of course he would help his birthplace Banje, and then Terpeze, Lladrovci, this is what I remember, while during the offensive, as I said, other villages on the eastern part and north-east from Berisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you about Lapusnik in particular. You've already indicated that Lapusnik was in the municipality of Gllogoc, which itself was in Drenica. So is it your evidence that Lapusnik came within the zone that in fact was most organised during April to August, namely Drenica?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: During that time, did you have occasion to go to Lapusnik yourself? Do you remember whether you did or not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been to Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We can see on this map, admittedly different on the ground, it's not that far away from your home village, is it, Negrovce, which is just to the north-west on the map you're looking at. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to take too long probably, but during that period of time, we gather from your evidence that you were moving around with the General Staff and as a spokesman quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I don't want -- you can give the places if you wish, but over what area were you moving during that time? Can you just give us some idea of the sort of places you went to so Their Honours can see the scope of where you travelled. Could you just indicate -- you can name the places if it's easier if you travelled as far -- I'm giving an illustration as Malisevo in the west or Zborce in the east and so on. If you can give us an idea of the parameters where you moved in this period of time.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We moved in Klecka when we gave interviews or had meetings. Then in Divjake, in Berisa. Between Divjake and Berisa there is another small village which is not marked here; it's name is Novo Selo. Then to Terpeze, Orlate. There is another village called Vuqak also not marked here. In the north we have Bajice. On the western side of Bajice is the village of Terdec. We moved to this place as well and we also came up to Drenoc villages which are on the northern-eastern part of the Skenderaj junction, Gllogoc-Skenderaj junction. We've moved to villages of the Vushtrri municipality, Mitrovic municipality, and Podujeva. I have been in the area covering the villages of Dukagjin and Suhareke. These were my movements in the capacity of a spokesmen at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the question I wanted to ask you in the light of that, did you at any time hear that there was located or said to be located in Lapusnik a prison camp?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I did not hear about it. And I say this with full responsibility that I have heard about the so-called camp, prison, after the arrest of Fatmir and his friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to ask you a further question, given your position within the General Staff. Would Lapusnik as a location in the April/August period have been a sensible place to situate a prison camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object on this, again based on foundation. The witness has said, number one, that he was not involved in operational matters; number two, that he did not even go to Lapusnik at this time. So for him to answer this question I think would be purely speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in my submission there are two parts to this. One, of course he said he hadn't been to Lapusnik in this period, and that was a precursor. However, from his answers he's travelled very widely indeed, and I submit and I don't think there was objection taken to me asking whether throughout those travels during this period he'd period of a prison camp; I leave to comment for later the significance of that. However, as far as the second part is concerned, here is somebody who is not concerned with operational matters, but that does not mean that he may not have a view about them, particularly as he is not only a spokesman but he must have been in very close contact on the General Staff level with those who did have concern for operations and he must have known from time to time where the front line of any exercise or operation occurred such that he then would be in a position, because he can't be without -- entirely without some military experience to know whether Lapusnik on the front line, as it was at one stage, was a sensible place to have a prison camp. That's our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, in view of the matters that have been indicated in the objection, could I indicate that the weight that would be attached to the answer is likely to be seen to be very little indeed. But I won't rule that you should not ask. You have a somewhat threadbare basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I understand the objection and I understand Your Honour's point. I'm obviously not going to waste Your Honour's time to ask questions that produce answers, so far as this aspect are concerned, as to whether it was a sensible place. I leave it for comment for later. I see the time. I wonder whether you were thinking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was waiting for you to appear to draw breath for the appropriate moment. We will break now and resume at 5 after 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm wondering if before the witness is brought back in to continue the cross-examination I could just raise a matter, a concern about a misimpression that I believe may have been left at the end of Mr. Topolski's cross-examination. I've already raised this matter with Mr. Topolski and he concurs with the problem and also with the solution. At the end of the cross-examination, and specifically it's at page 16, the witness asserted that he had "facts to support the proposition that people have been processed before giving evidence to the Prosecutors of this Tribunal by Serb intelligence services." We then, in order to give the witness an opportunity to provide these facts, we went into closed [sic] session. And my concern that the misimpression that this leaves for the public watching the trial. And I would ask - and again, Mr. Topolski concurs with this - that the record be made clear in public that in fact the witness offered no such facts to support that proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And are you proposing that what you have just said should be that public recording of that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that would be sufficient. Perhaps also that there be no harm in making that portion that was in private session public session. I see no reason for it to be in private session. And just so the record is absolutely clear, it could be made un -- made open, made public for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say that nothing was said in the closed session. I think that may be the way to do it, Mr. Whiting, simply order to be opened that which was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that's an excellent solution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Something about jack-in-the-box. We'll have the witness. Thank you for that, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, the last question I want to ask you, although it may take a little time to answer it, is to take up your offer earlier this afternoon that you could in fact indicate to the Tribunal in the April-to-August period of 1998 the development of the subzones into operational and active zones. We've dealt with Drenica, which you've indicated was the most operative and you put Pastrik in the middle. But what I'd like to do now with your help and your offer is to just run through the other zones. I think in terms of -- this is not particularly controversial, I hope. Drenica was commanded by someone called Selimi. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And you've already indicated the municipalities involved in that. So I pass from that. And if I'm wrong in what I put, please correct me. Would the second one be on the basis of what you -- second subzone of what you've already said -- Dukagjin just to the south and west, would that be the next subzone in terms of development? If not, please say which one it would be.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was subzone number 3 and later zone number 3 [as interpreted]. And it came immediately after Drenica zone from the organizational point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to pause. I'm just wondering looking at the answer whether there's been a misunderstanding. It says: "Yes, that was subzone number 3 and later zone number 3." Was it -- I'm sorry to just ask. Is that right? Was it subzone something else and later zone number 3?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Same thing, yes. Who was the commander of that zone as you recall it, again in this period of time, April to August? If you can help by remembering.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The zone commander, he was such later. But at this period it was Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And since it's close by, are you in a position to indicate the municipalities in this case that were embraced by this zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you just indicate what they are.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the zone was Istog lying to the north part of Dukagjin; Peja, Decan, Gjurakoc, and part of Klina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. So in terms of organisation after that subzone numbered 3, what came next in this period of time again?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very similar to those ranking from Pastrik and Shala of Bajgora, then Llap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And who was in charge -- can I take Shale first of all. Who was in charge of that one during this period?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rrahman Rama [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And you've mentioned Pastrik. Who was in charge of that one?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In charge of Pastrik there were different persons. Initially it was Musa Jashari. Later it was Ekrem Rexha. And finally, Tahir Sinani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You've mentioned three individuals there. Are those three individuals who took over one after another all during the April-to-August period?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April to August -- not from April but it was by the end of July was Musa Jashari in charge until November, if I recollect. Then after November came Ekrem Rexha. And it was sometime in March or April 1999 that Tahir Sinani became the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I just -- pausing on the Pastrik subzone for the moment, does it follow from what you're saying that there wasn't in fact anybody in overall command between - I'm sorry to be particular about the months - April to July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And just in this case, I won't do it in all cases, but in this case the Pastrik subzone as you understood it, what municipalities were involved here in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Malisheve; Rahovec; of Prizren; of Sharri, the former Dragash; and the municipality of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now the other zone you put on a par with Shale and Pastrik was Llap. Can I ask you about that? Who was in charge of that zone in this period, at some stage in this period that is?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main person in charge for that zone was Rrustem Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, we I think have only got two subzones left to go. Is, therefore, I make it number 6, Nerodime?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And in relation to that at what point between April and August was there somebody with overall command in that zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around July or maybe early August that the commander of this zone was Shukri Buja. But I have to say here that this is a zone that lied [as interpreted] in the north-east of Shari Mountains and it should comprise the municipalities of Shtime, Lipjan, Ferizaj, and Kacanik . But because of geographical conditions I think, the army was organised only in the villages of the municipalities lying at the foot of Shari Mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: That leaves us I think with one more subzone to go, Karadak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And again, at what stage in this same period did someone appear to be in command there?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the zone that we might say was less engaged in military operational activity. The commander of this zone was appointed at the end of 1998 or the beginning of 1999, Ahmet Isufi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I represent Haradin Bala. I'm going to ask you questions in one area and one area alone - I have no desire to go over the areas that have been ably covered by my colleagues - and that deals with the area of the civilian population that was displaced during the summer months of 1998. You mentioned that in the valleys of Berisa Mountain, the valleys above the villages of Kishna Reka, Nekovce, Bajice, Shale, and Kroimire, there was somewhere in the neighbourhood of 60 to 70.000 displaced people, villagers who had been driven from their villages as a result of the Serbian offensive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us when the displacement began? And by that, what months did people start to have to three their homes as a result of the Serbian movement?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The displacement of people from their homes began first in the half of -- in the half of July, especially in Rahovec. Then with the stepping-up of the enemy offensive in August and September, the population were forced to flee their homes and settle in -- along the valleys and mountains. This happened in Berisa Mountains. On the opposite side of the asphalt road, that is in the Drenica villages, situated in Ternez and Dupcak villages, Bajice valley, Verbovc Mountains and in a plain called Molv [phoen] plain. The villagers left their homes and settled in places where they could have the -- some strategic support. This went on during all the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that "the villagers settled in places where they could have some strategic support," who was taking care of the villagers that were coming in this rapid influx into this area?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people of KLA, the members of KLA, were the ones who were mainly protecting the people because they their families were among these displaced people. So the soldiers had on the other hand to fight and on the other to take care of the families and to take them to safer places.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it fair to say then that during what you have called the middle phase of the KLA at a time when there was a lack of infrastructure, a lack of resources, funds, arms, and communication facilities or possibilities, that among other things that were exacerbating the situation that were making it difficult for people to operate, was among this major influx of displaced people?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. And the KLA leaders of course had to support the civilian population to assist them. And so this many cases they gave them the surplus food they had displaced civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a few questions and you'll be finished unless the Court has some questions. You mentioned today in your testimony -- you made -- you answered a question or two about the FARK. Do you remember that, talking about the FARK?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the FARK a part of the KLA or was it a separate organisation?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I need some time to explain this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if you could answer the question first and then give your explanation, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was another organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if you have a brief explanation, please provide it.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1991/1992 I think. Former officers of the Yugoslav army, meaning Albanian officers, were organised by the government of Bujar Bukoshi who was -- had a government in exile. He tried to set up an army with such people, but the Serb secret service found out very soon what they were going to do and arrested some of them. Some others left Kosova and lived in the Western countries. After the outbreak of the war, the cadres of that former attempt to set up that army who regarded themselves as professional cadres regrouped to enter Kosova. Negotiations were held with them, and they agreed to come to Kosova as military experts and to fight under the logo of the KLA. But in fact they tried to maintain their links, their old links because of the schools, the educations with the Bikoshi government who paid these people. So this formation caused great harm to the KLA. I have explained this in another session, that such people have handed over to the Serb forces some 5.000 or 6.000 weapons. And they have withdrawn -- part of their army withdrew in Albania. It was at the end of August or beginning of September 1998 that some 50 soldiers were left of them. This is more or less the explanation I want to give about -- a brief explanation I want to give about FARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Tahir Zemi, was he a member of the FARK?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I believe you testified in a previous session, and perhaps it was in reference to what you've just explained, that Tahir Zemi operated in the Dukagjin zone during the summer months of 1998. Was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from the Dukagjin zone, did the FARK, to your knowledge, operate anywhere else, or were they limited to the Dukagjin zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were FARK members also outside of Dukagjin, but they had limited possibilities to act. Therefore, they -- by the end of 1998 they ceased their activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where outside of Dukagjin, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They operated in -- mostly in the Pastrik zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where in the Pastrik zone, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially in Therande, former Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some questions today about the fighting in Rahovec and you testified that the fighting was unauthorised by the General Staff and also, as I understand it, that it was spontaneous. And I want to ask you some questions about that. When the KLA took control of Rahovec for a brief time, was that the first time that the KLA had taken control of a major town in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first town that KLA took under its control. A small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know who led the KLA forces in that attack on Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rahovec had its own unit which operated until that time outside the city. The leaders of that unit when the attack happened were not there; they were neither in Rahovec nor in Kosova. At that time the General Staff had appointed two military men to see what possibilities there were for the operational -- for the operations of the KLA, Agim Cela --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to sound out the situation in the terrain to see what they could do they went to Rahovec. And the instructions they gave to the Rahovec unit was not to enter the city because the KLA was not prepared from the defence aspect to protect the city with weapons, so they shouldn't enter the city. I said the same thing during the first session. This happened in Bardhi i Madh, in Obiliq mine, which was one of the closest settlements to Pristina. They were told also that because of the limited number of weapons that we had especially to protect the settlement there, Bardhi i Madh was not a mountainous terrain so it was not easy for the KLA to defend it. But both attacks took place without the approval of the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But who then led the attack on Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first the city taken was Rahovec unit, which I don't remember what name it had, but I know that there was an officer with a pseudonym Piktori was that. He was a cadre educated in the military school of Yugoslavia, but I don't have more information to give about that person. What I know is that the attack went on without the approval of the General Staff. After the city was taken, then the General Staff appointed Agim Cela to lead the defence of Rahovec. This was a quick decision and very severe fight took place, during which the leader Agim Cela that was appointed by the General Staff was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the battle of Rahovec, did you ever hear anything about some 40-plus Serb civilians being captured during the battle and disappearing, never to be seen again? Did you ever hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not heard anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you ever heard anything about the 121 Brigade being in existence at that time and participating in the fighting at Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the fighting took place in Rahovec, brigades were not yet named or formed for that matter. Just to give you an example, Brigade 121 is named after Ismet Jashari, whose pseudonym was Kumanova, and he was killed by the end of August. It was 25th or 26th of August; I am not sure. But it was the end of August. So a brigade could not be named after him before he was killed, which means that it was called after him after his death in the fighting with the Serb military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before the 121 Brigade was known as the Kumanova Brigade, was it known by another name?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your knowledge was it known as just the 121 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying again that brigades were not formed in Pastrik zone before the summer offensive, which means before August. Before August some attempts were made to form brigades in the zones of Drenica and Dukagjin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to pass to a different subject. You described the division between the Drenica zone and the Dukagjin zone. And I just want to see if I understand your testimony correctly. Did you -- is it your testimony that the Klina municipality was divided between those two zones, part of Klina was in Drenica and part of Klina was in the Dukagjin zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was it. They were divided in some instances by the road axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that leads very well to my next question. With respect to the division between the Drenica zone and the Pastrik zone, did you ever hear that the division between those two zones was the Peja-Pristina highway, that that represented the division between the two zones? Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire road. Pristina-Peja didn't divide the zone, Drenica and Dukagjin. I want to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kline, meaning before you enter the bridge to Kline, on the left side when you go to Peja there is the road that goes to Gjurakoc. Going in the direction of Gjurakoc, the villages situated on the left side of this road were involved in the Pastrik zone. When you enter Kline there are two roads. One road leads to Gjurakoc and Istog and this was the dividing line of Drenica from Dukagjin. If you go from Kline to Gjurakoc the villages lying on the left side belong to Dukagjin zone. The villages on the right side belong to the Drenica zone. This road from Kline to Gjurakoc and Istog crosses the Mitrovic-Peja road. And again, this road Mitrovic-Peja was a dividing line. If you go from Peja to Mitrovic from Gjurakoc on the right side was the Drenica zone. On the left side was part of Dukagjin zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a part of the road that you did not address, and that is the part of the road from the Pristina to the Orlate junction. At the Orlate junction one road goes to Peja and one road goes to Rahovec. That part of the road from Pristina to the Orlate junction, did you ever hear that that was the dividing line between Drenica and Pastrik?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not the entire road. I'm mentioning even the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, focusing -- let me put the question and then maybe we can get clarity on this. Focusing on that part of the road between Orlate and Pristina, what portion of that road divided the Pastrik zone from the Drenica zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road is not what divides the Pastrik zone from Drenica zone, but the Prishtine-Peja road near Arlat is another road that goes to Malisheve and Rahovec. And on both sides of this road there is Arlat village. Arlat village was part of Drenica zone. Then there is the Lapusnik village, which is also divided in two parts. There are three large neighbourhoods with different names which are known by the local people, but officially it is known as a single village by the name of Lapusnik. It's Lapusnik neighbourhood, Paterk and Vukofc neighbourhoods. This entire village was part of Drenica zone. Then come the villages that are found in the north-eastern part of Berisa Mountains like Komorane, Kishna Reka, and Nekovce; they were part -- or part of the military organisation of Drenica zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like other villages, Fushtice, Sankovc that are in the eastern part. So I want to say that not the entire roads divided zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me focus you specifically on Lapusnik. Did you hear that in fact part of Lapusnik was divided and part of Lapusnik was in Drenica and part of Lapusnik was in Pastrik? Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I remember, the entire Lapusnik was part -- even Arlat, even though it was found on the opposite side of the road it was also part of Drenica zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that Sulejman Selimi during -- from May to July of 1998 was the commander of the Drenica zone. Have you ever talked to him about where the dividing line was between the Drenica zone and the Pastrik zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The responsibilities and -- the level of responsibility of Sulejman Selimi was not determined by the zones. The zones were divided -- determined by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was: Have you ever talked to him about where the dividing line was between the Drenica zone and the Pastrik zone? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not talk because I thought he knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I'm going to move to a different subject and it's the last subject. During your cross-examination you gave a definition or attempted to give a definition about what it means to be a collaborator. My question to you is: During the various pronouncements that were made by the General Staff during 1998 - and I include communiques, speeches, political declarations, and interviews that you gave - was any such definition of a collaborator ever provided by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then my final question, sir, is: You were asked some questions on cross-examination about what procedures, if any, were followed to determine who was a collaborator. And I'll put the same question to you on this topic, which is: Again, in these various pronouncements that were made - speeches, communiques, interviews, political declarations - did the General Staff ever communicate procedures that should be followed to determine who is and who is not a collaborator? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with the explanation of the word "collaborator" because we thought at that time and we think today that it is something that is well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could answer my last question, sir, I would appreciate it. Were -- did the General Staff ever communicate procedures that should be followed to determine who is a collaborator, yes or no, during 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Krasniqi. You'll be pleased to know that that concludes your evidence. Thank you for the assistance you've given and you are now free to return to your home. Could I ask you to take with you one thought: Witnesses in this case and in many other cases are permitted by order of this Tribunal to give evidence under a pseudonym. That occurs after this Tribunal has been satisfied by material placed before it that there is reason for that person to seek protection from the publication of his name or her name and other identifying material. In this case, any witness who has so far or who will give evidence under a pseudonym does so by order of this Chamber. In no case is that order given because of the consideration which you identified in your evidence. I think that might help you as you reflect in later time on the proceedings here if you knew that. Thank you very much indeed, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Black will be handling the next witness, who is prepared and is ready to testify. If I could be briefly excused and I will return in a few moments, but Mr. Black can carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd call the next Prosecution witness, Ms. Susanne Ringgaard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the affirmation which is on the card now handed to you.
